::: {.paper-status}
Job market paper · Working paper, September 2026 · 87 pages including the Internet Appendix
:::

::: {.standfirst}
Asset managers keep adding stock characteristics to the libraries behind their return forecasts. Copying characteristics they already have, or reweighting whole themes, adds no information, yet on U.S. stocks it still moves a tuned portfolio rule's economic tilts and stock holdings. Whether that helps or hurts depends on the method, trading costs and how missing returns are valued, while adding genuinely new characteristics has small and uncertain effects on forecast accuracy.
:::

## The question {#question}

**When a characteristic library changes without gaining information, does a tuned investment rule still change, and does the change reach holdings and net returns?**

Repeating a column adds no observation and leaves the set of reachable linear portfolios unchanged. But a regularized estimator charges a penalty per coefficient, so copies make a theme cheaper to use, even after the penalty is tuned again <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Introduction; Section I.B">(Introduction; Section I.B)</span>. The paper measures how large this effect is for four tuned portfolio methods. It follows the effect from the estimated weights to economic themes, named stocks and returns after costs.

## Why it matters {#why}

Managers update these libraries routinely <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Introduction">(Introduction)</span>. The widely used Jensen–Kelly–Pedersen library has 153 characteristics in 13 themes <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section II.A">(Section II.A)</span>, and overlap within themes is uneven. Quality has 17 columns but a correlation participation rank of only 3.47, a rough count of distinct directions in the data (not of independent information sources); seasonality has 12 columns and a rank of 11.78 <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section III.A; Table II">(paper, Section III.A; Table II)</span>. If a better backtest can come from how inputs are written down rather than from what they measure, then a library update needs a different kind of check.

- **Economic.** A manager may read a new tilt toward, say, value as new evidence about value. Part of it can be a bookkeeping effect of the library.
- **Practical.** Tilts become trades. Trades cost money, so a change in representation can change net returns even when gross returns barely move.
- **Statistical.** A lower test error does not prove that new inputs carry new information. A tuned rule can improve because its penalty changed.

## The argument at a glance {#map}

::: {.logic-map}
1. **Question.** Does an information-preserving change to the library change a tuned investment rule? → [The question](#question)
2. **Why.** Library updates are routine, and their value is usually judged by backtests that cannot separate information from reweighting. → [Why it matters](#why)
3. **Framework.** Exact copies and theme rescaling keep the data and the reachable portfolios fixed, so any response belongs to the fitted procedure. → [The framework](#framework)
4. **Mechanism.** Copying a theme divides its effective ridge penalty by the number of copies, which tilts the fit toward that theme. → [A simple example](#example)
5. **Evidence.** Theme balancing moves theme attribution by 0.20 to 0.27 and stock targets by 0.19 to 0.28 of gross exposure <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Introduction; Table I">(paper, Table I)</span>; net payoffs depend on method and costs; real expansion from 39 to 153 characteristics has small, uncertain effects. → [Design and main results](#results)
6. **Contribution.** An empirical diagnostic that follows a library update through attribution, holdings and cost-dependent returns. → [How it relates to prior work](#literature)
7. **Boundary.** The design is diagnostic: no investable-performance claim and no optimal library. → [Scope](#scope)
:::

## The framework {#framework}

The design holds the investment method, the eligible stocks and the decision dates fixed and changes only the library <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Introduction">(Introduction)</span>. Two controlled changes carry no new information. **Selective copies** give every column of one theme five total copies. **Theme balancing** rescales each theme's columns by its column count, so a theme with many columns no longer gets more room under the penalty than a theme with few. The mechanism is one line of algebra. If a characteristic is replaced by $m$ identical columns with coefficients $\theta_j$ that add up to $b$, the cheapest way to split $b$ gives

$$
\min_{\sum_j \theta_j = b} \; \sum_{j=1}^{m} \theta_j^2 \;=\; \frac{b^2}{m}.
$$

So a ridge penalty on the copies charges only $1/m$ of the usual price for the same exposure <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section I.B, equation 2">(Section I.B, equation 2)</span>. For stock ridge there is an exact control: scale the copies' penalty back up ("transport" it) and the original problem returns <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section I.B">(Section I.B)</span>.

Every estimate is then mapped back to the 153 original characteristics and scored in the same 13 themes <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section III.B">(Section III.B)</span>. A theme's weight is its share of the fitted payoff's variance,

$$
s_g = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(u_g, u)}{\operatorname{Var}(u)},
$$

where $u_g$ is theme $g$'s payoff and $u$ the total. The shares add up to one and can be negative when a theme hedges <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section I.D, equation 4">(Section I.D, equation 4)</span>. The change in attribution is half the sum of absolute share changes. The paper compares it with the change in stock targets and in returns after costs, because each measures a different consequence.

## A simple example {#example}

{{< include /_includes/_exhibit-helpers.qmd >}}

::: {#figure-jmp-toy .column-body-outset .dfigure .toy role="figure" aria-labelledby="figure-jmp-toy-title"}
<div class="dfigure-title" id="figure-jmp-toy-title"><strong>Figure 1: Illustrative example, copying a theme without new information.</strong> Two characteristics, one per theme, equally useful by construction.</div>

{{< include _fig-jmp-toy.qmd >}}

<div class="figcaption"><strong>How to read it.</strong> Illustrative example, not the paper's data. Characteristic X (theme X) and characteristic Z (theme Z) are standardized, have correlation ρ, and each has a true coefficient of 0.5. A ridge rule with penalty λ is fitted on population moments. Copying X k times with an ordinary penalty on each copy is the same as cutting X's penalty to λ/k <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section I.B, equation 2">(Section I.B, equation 2)</span>. The solid line shows theme X's share of fitted payoff variance, as in equation 4; the dashed line applies the transported penalty. "Error above best fit" is the population prediction error in excess of the unpenalized fit. <span class="provenance">Source: computed in the browser from the formulas in Sections I.B and I.D of the paper; no data file.</span></div>
:::

Start at k = 1: the two themes get equal weight and each explains half the fitted variance. Now raise the copies slider: the data do not change, yet weight moves from Z to X and X's share reaches 73% at the default settings, while the dashed transported control stays at 50%. The prediction error in the last column falls as copies are added, because in this population toy any positive penalty is too strong and the copies weaken it.

In finite samples with retuning, copies can help or hurt <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section V.A">(Section V.A)</span>, so a better test score is not proof of new information <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section V.C; Table VII">(paper, Section V.C; Table VII)</span>. Raise λ and the shift grows; with a tiny λ the copies hardly matter. Here λ is held fixed; the paper chooses it again, and the shift survives because one penalty number cannot undo copies of a single theme <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section I.B">(Section I.B)</span>.

## Design and main results {#results}

The library is the Jensen–Kelly–Pedersen database of 153 U.S. characteristics in 13 themes [@jensen2023replication], extracted in May 2026 <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section II.A">(Section II.A)</span>. There are 179 monthly decisions from January 2011 to November 2025, each estimated on the previous 120 months, with returns through December 2025 <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section II.C">(Section II.C)</span>. The four methods are blocked ridge, a training-Sharpe-weighted ridge (SR-weighted) adapted from @ke2025alignment, Universal Portfolio Shrinkage (UPSA) [@kelly2026upsa], and the leave-one-out (LOO) ridge inside UPSA's code <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section III.B">(Section III.B)</span>. One allocation rule turns every estimate into stock positions: a 10% volatility target and a gross exposure cap of two. Stock-level ledgers then charge costs of 10 to 100 basis points per traded dollar <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Sections IV.A and IV.C">(Sections IV.A and IV.C)</span>.

<div class="dfigure-title" id="table-jmp-1-title"><strong>Table 1: Theme balancing changes tilts and holdings in all four methods.</strong> Paper Table I, original (O) and theme-balanced (B) libraries.</div>

::: {.table-scroll .tbl-num}
| Method | Attribution change | Holdings change | Gross Sharpe, O | Gross Sharpe, B |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Blocked ridge | 0.231 | 0.277 | 0.366 | 0.348 |
| SR-weighted ridge | 0.198 | 0.239 | 0.490 | 0.397 |
| LOO ridge | 0.271 | 0.227 | 1.003 | 1.105 |
| UPSA | 0.274 | 0.191 | 1.126 | 1.141 |
:::

<div class="figcaption">Attribution change: monthly average of half the summed absolute change in the 13 theme variance shares. Holdings change: gap between the two sets of stock targets as a share of their average gross exposure; it is not realized turnover. Sharpe ratios are annualized and before costs <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Table I">(paper, Table I)</span>. <span class="provenance">Source: Characteristic Libraries and Portfolio Decisions, Table I.</span></div>

::: {.takeaway}
**What this shows.** Rebalancing the themes, with no new data, changes what the rule holds. Theme attribution moves by 0.20 to 0.27, and stock targets move by 19% to 28% of average gross exposure <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Introduction; Table I">(paper, Introduction; Table I)</span>. Gross Sharpe ratios rise for two methods and fall for the other two. So the representation matters, but it has no single direction of benefit.
:::

::: {#figure-jmp-cost .column-body-outset .dfigure role="figure" aria-labelledby="figure-jmp-cost-title"}
<div class="dfigure-title" id="figure-jmp-cost-title"><strong>Figure 2: Cost sensitivity of a fixed allocation rule.</strong> Paper Figure 3, with a cost slider.</div>

{{< include _fig-jmp-cost.qmd >}}

<div class="figcaption"><strong>How to read it.</strong> Each panel is one method; each line is one library. Move the slider to a cost level. The paper reports exact results at 0, 10, 25, 50 and 100 basis points; at any other level the table and the open markers show a straight-line interpolation between the neighbouring exact points, and the table says so. Figure note from the paper: "Each panel varies one-way costs per traded dollar for the original representation, theme balancing and fivefold value replication. The vertical axis is annual arithmetic mean excess return in percent. Each rate has a separate self-financing cash and return-drift account; target-weight rules remain fixed. The stock gross cap is two and primary missing outcomes receive zero vendor excess return. The curves do not include optimized trade scheduling, borrow fees or market impact." <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Figure 3">(paper, Figure 3)</span> Before costs, LOO ridge and UPSA earn about 4.5% to 5.1% a year <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Table IV">(paper, Table IV)</span>. At 25 basis points, balancing lowers UPSA's mean to 0.92%, a difference of −0.19 points whose 95% interval, [−0.57, 0.19], includes zero; five seasonality copies cut the SR-weighted ridge's mean by 1.30 points, with a band of [−2.35, −0.25] that holds jointly across its 13 copy experiments <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section III.D">(Section III.D)</span>. <span class="provenance">Source: Characteristic Libraries and Portfolio Decisions, Figure 3 and Table IV; results file summary.csv.</span> <a href="/data/jmp_cost_sensitivity.json">Data</a></div>
:::

::: {.takeaway}
**What this shows.** Trading costs take most of the gross return. All four original books trade 1.13 to 1.28 dollars per dollar of capital a month <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Table V">(paper, Table V)</span>, so at 25 basis points original UPSA's mean falls from 4.79% to 1.10% a year <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section IV.C; Table IV">(paper, Section IV.C; Table IV)</span>. Library changes then shift net returns by amounts that are mostly within sampling error; the caption gives the one clearly adverse case.
:::

The paper then asks the opposite question: what do real new characteristics add? Growing monthly ridge from 39 to 153 characteristics raises normalized prediction loss, measured relative to the loss of a zero forecast, by 0.0079 percentage points. That is a slight deterioration, but the 95% interval of [−0.040, 0.068] allows both gains and losses <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section V.A">(Section V.A)</span>. The plain historical mean does slightly better than either library: out-of-sample R² of 0.239%, against 0.214% with 39 characteristics and 0.206% with 153 <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section V.A; Table VI">(paper, Section V.A; Table VI)</span>.

::: {.column-body-outset}
<div class="dfigure-title" id="figure-jmp-omit-title"><strong>Figure 3: Leaving out one theme at a time.</strong> Paper Figure 4.</div>

![](/assets/img/characteristic-libraries/figure4-omissions.png){width="600" fig-alt="Dot-and-interval chart. For each of the 13 themes, the change in normalized prediction loss when that theme is dropped from the 153-characteristic library. All points lie between about minus 0.007 and plus 0.026 percentage points, and every light simultaneous band crosses zero."}

<div class="figcaption"><strong>How to read it.</strong> Each row drops one theme from the full library and refits the ridge forecast. Points to the right of zero mean the forecast got worse without that theme. Dark bars are pointwise 95% intervals; light bands hold jointly across all 13 themes. Figure note from the paper: "An omission removes shared and distinct content together." <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Figure 4">(paper, Figure 4)</span> <span class="provenance">Source: Characteristic Libraries and Portfolio Decisions, Figure 4 (p. 34 of the PDF).</span></div>
:::

::: {.takeaway}
**What this shows.** No single theme is reliably needed for the forecast. Dropping quality has the largest point estimate, raising loss by about 0.026 points, yet every simultaneous band includes zero <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section V.A; Figure 4">(paper, Section V.A; Figure 4)</span>. That does not mean the themes carry no information. It means this procedure, on this sample, extracts too little to measure precisely. Real additions and the copy controls answer different questions, and the paper keeps them apart.
:::

## How it relates to prior work {#literature}

Shrinkage and regularization are now standard tools for building portfolios from many characteristics. The closest studies compare methods on a given library. This paper holds each method fixed and changes only how the library is written down.

::: {.lit-table .table-scroll}
| Prior work | What it established | What this paper adds |
|:--|:--|:--|
| @kozak2020shrinking | Shrinkage of characteristic-portfolio weights gives robust out-of-sample stochastic discount factors. | Shows that the same kind of penalty responds to how the library is represented, and traces that response into holdings. |
| @kelly2026upsa | UPSA combines ridge portfolios to target out-of-sample performance and groups weights into economic themes. | Keeps UPSA's public code fixed and changes its inputs; balancing shifts UPSA's theme shares by a distance of 0.274 <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Table I">(paper, Table I)</span>. |
| @jensen2023replication | Builds a public library of 153 factors in 13 themes and finds that most factors replicate, including out of sample and across 93 countries. | Uses that library as the object of study: its uneven within-theme overlap motivates the controls. |
| @jensen2026implementable | Portfolios should be judged net of trading costs; cost-aware learning improves the implementable frontier. | Uses a fixed, non-optimized allocation rule and explicit cost ledgers to show that library changes reach net returns; a cost-aware optimizer like theirs could change the response <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section IV.A">(Section IV.A)</span>. |
| @choueifaty2013properties; @george2010dilution | Duplication invariance in portfolio construction; priors that correct for redundant models. | Supplies an empirical measure of how far tuned procedures depart from such invariance, from themes to named stocks. |
| @ke2025alignment | Setting each asset's shrinkage strength by its Sharpe ratio (Sharpe Ratio Shrinkage) can improve high-dimensional portfolios when profitability differs across assets. | Uses an adaptation of this rule as one of the four methods and shows that it too responds to representation: five seasonality copies lower its 25 bp mean by 1.30 points <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section III.D">(Section III.D)</span>. |
| @kelly2024virtue | Richer, more complex models can improve return prediction; @nagel2025seemingly questions how general this is. | Studies exact copies, which add no new function; the paper does not test the broader complexity argument. |
:::

The angle is empirical and narrow on purpose. The identities behind the controls are known. What is new is measuring how much four tuned procedures respond on a common panel, and following the response to stock positions and cost-dependent returns <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Introduction">(Introduction)</span>. The result is a diagnostic a manager can run before adopting a library update: check the fitted attribution, the stock targets and the net payoff under the chosen implementation. Theme balancing is offered as a transparent alternative weighting, not as the right one. Companion papers study characteristic geometry in portfolio choice ([Characteristic Geometry and Portfolio Choice](characteristic-geometry.qmd)) and metric-based identification in factor models ([Characteristic-Space Metrics in Factor Models](characteristic-space-metrics.qmd)).

## Scope {#scope}

- The paper makes no claim of investable performance. Costs exclude borrow fees and market impact, and under a spread-based cost proxy all three UPSA versions have negative means <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section IV.C">(Section IV.C)</span>. Returns also depend on how missing returns are valued: before fees, original UPSA's mean is 4.79% under the primary valuation but ranges from 0.62% to 8.98% when positions with unobserved returns are valued at +100% or −100% total return. These are scenarios, not bounds <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section IV.C">(Section IV.C)</span>.
- It does not identify an optimal library, and it does not show that theme balancing is better.
- It does not claim that the added characteristics lack information. Small, uncertain forecast effects describe these procedures only <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section V.A; Section VII">(Section V.A; Section VII)</span>.
- The data are a retrospective U.S. extraction that was also used to develop the design, which was not preregistered <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section II.F; Section VI.D">(Section II.F; Section VI.D)</span>.
- Intervals condition on the fitted decisions, and an interval that contains zero does not establish equivalence <span class="loc" title="Working paper, September 2026: Section VI.A">(Section VI.A)</span>.
